title: The Fields Before Ownership Learned to Speak

features.name: fence post at the boundary
features.desc-on-touch: you run your palm along the splintered wood, feeling where the land on one side of your touch belongs to someone, and the land on the other side belongs to someone else. the post doesn't feel the difference.

features.name: property marker stone
features.desc-on-touch: numbers carved in 1952 still legible; the coordinates no longer match any reference system still in use.

features.name: where you kneel to read the grass
features.desc-on-touch: the shortest plants grow here—clover, wire-grass, small herbs—crowded tight enough that they have learned each other's names. they don't ask which side of the fence they grow on.

features.name: the horizon as evidence
features.desc-on-touch: from here, the land appears to continue uninterrupted. the fence runs perpendicular to your eye. ownership becomes a line you drew in the air, visible only if you stand exactly here.

inscription: the fence learned it was only a line; the roots learned it was no line at all

reverie.title: REVERIE — walking the boundary at dusk
narr: you both walk the fence line as the light flattens,
stepping from one side of the property to the other,
and she says: ownership is just a language the earth
stopped speaking. the roots knew that. the grass never
learned it in the first place. you hold the fence post
and feel how it's rotting into the ground it divides.
